newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel head opposes savings tax.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel head opposes savings tax.

text.p: Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel said on Sunday he opposed a recommendation to tax savings of less than 10 years at a time when the government needed to stimulate the level of national savings.

Frenkel voiced his opposition at a special cabinet meeting convened to discuss capital market reform recommendations made by a committee headed by Treasury Director General David Brodett. A tax on short- and medium-term savings as a way of long-term savings is the most controversial proposal.

"Imposing a new tax on certain types of savings could bring about a decline in national savings and growth in private consumption, particularly in light of the great uncertainty concerning the capital market and the various savings instruments," Frenkel was quoted as saying in a statement from the central bank.
"The influence of a new tax...could heighten the uncertainty and this is not desirable in a period characterised by a decline in savings and lack of certainty."
The cabinet is expected to continue its debate on the reform measures, which are backed by Finance Minister Dan Meridor, at 1600 GMT.
Frenkel said the committee's report did not provide an estimate for the impact of the various changes on tax receipts, the budget and national savings.

He said he supported the committee's recommendation to stimulate long-term savings by a lowering of taxes, but only if ways could be found to guarantee that the government would not deviate from its budget deficit targets.
A senior central bank director, David Klein, was a member of the Brodett committee.

Frenkel said he backed most of the committee's recommendations, which also seek to stimulate investment in the stock and bond market. He said he supported Klein's position that the government should stop issuing non-tradeable high-yielding bonds for pension funds.

If this is not possible, Frenkel said he supported the committee's proposal to reduce the amount pension funds can invest in such bonds as a way of encouraging the funds to invest more in the capital market.
The absence of pension funds in the Israeli market renders the market more vulnerable to sharp swings, Frenkel said.
